definition: A priest, teacher, and judge in ancient Celtic society, believed to hold deep knowledge of nature, law, and the sacred.
origin: Druid comes from Gaulish "druides", most likely built from Proto-Celtic roots meaning "oak" and "to know" — an "oak-knower" reflecting the sacred role oak trees and oak groves played in Celtic ritual. Roman writers such as Julius Caesar and Pliny the Elder described druids as the learned class of Gaulish and British society, serving as priests, judges, and keepers of oral law and astronomy. The Old Irish form "drui" carried the same meaning into early Irish literature, where druids appear as advisors to kings and workers of magic.

definition: A professional poet and singer in Celtic society who composed and performed verse praising heroes, chronicling history, and satirizing enemies.
origin: Bard derives from Gaulish "bardos", from a Proto-Celtic root shared across Celtic languages, entering English via Scottish Gaelic and Irish "bard". Bards held a formal, often hereditary rank below the druids, trained for years in complex metre and genealogy so they could recite a chieftain's lineage and deeds from memory. A skilled bard could also compose a satire so cutting it was believed to raise blisters on its target's face, making bards figures both honoured and feared.

definition: An ancient Gaelic festival marking the end of the harvest and the beginning of winter, observed around the 31st of October and 1st of November.
origin: Samhain comes from Old Irish "samain", likely rooted in "sam" (summer) and a word for "end", marking the turning point when summer gave way to the dark half of the year. The Gaels believed the boundary between the world of the living and the Otherworld grew thin at Samhain, allowing spirits to cross over, and communities lit bonfires and left out food to appease wandering souls. Christian missionaries later placed All Saints' and All Souls' Day nearby, and Samhain's customs of costumes, bonfires, and offerings to the dead survived into the modern festival of Halloween.

definition: A Gaelic festival celebrated around the 1st of May marking the beginning of summer, traditionally observed with bonfires and rituals for fertility and protection.
origin: Beltane comes from Old Irish "Beltaine", widely thought to combine a word related to a bright or fire deity with "tene" (fire) — literally something like "bright fire". Cattle were driven between two bonfires at Beltane in a purification ritual meant to protect the herd before it was moved to summer pasture. The festival marked the midpoint between spring equinox and summer solstice, standing opposite Samhain on the Celtic wheel of the year, and its bonfire customs still survive in modern Gaelic revival festivals such as the Edinburgh Beltane Fire Festival.

definition: A powerful Irish goddess associated with war, fate, and death, often appearing as a crow or raven over battlefields.
origin: Morrigan (Old Irish "Mórrígan") is usually parsed as "mór" (great) plus "rígan" (queen), giving "great queen", though some scholars connect the first element to a root for terror or nightmare instead. Rather than a single goddess, "the Morrígan" sometimes names a trio of war-goddesses working together, reflecting how fluid identity could be in Irish myth.

definition: An Irish goddess of fire, poetry, healing, and smithcraft, whose worship later merged with the Christian Saint Brigid of Kildare.
origin: Brigid comes from Old Irish "Brigit", from a Proto-Celtic root meaning "the exalted one" or "high one", marking her as a goddess of high status among the Tuatha Dé Danann. She presided over poetry, healing wells, and the forge, a triple domain that made her one of the most widely venerated deities in pre-Christian Ireland. When Ireland converted, many of Brigid's associations — her feast day at the start of February, her sacred flame, and her healing wells — were carried over almost intact onto Saint Brigid of Kildare.

origin: Kelpie first appears in Scots in the 18th century, and though its exact roots are debated, many scholars connect it to Scottish Gaelic "colpach", meaning a young horse or heifer, fitting the creature's most common disguise. Tales describe the kelpie's coat as always dripping wet, and any rider foolish enough to mount it would find their hands stuck fast as it plunged into a loch or river. The legend likely served a practical purpose too, warning children away from dangerous water.

Unlike the more sinister fairies of other traditions, pixies were generally viewed as playful rather than dangerous.

definition: A supernatural being of folklore with magical powers, often small in size and capable of helping or harming humans.
origin: Fairy comes from Old French "faerie", meaning enchantment or the land of fairies, itself from Latin "fata", the Fates, the three goddesses who spun and cut the thread of human destiny. The word entered Middle English describing not individual creatures but a state of enchantment, and only later narrowed to mean the beings themselves. Celtic-speaking regions had their own older names for such beings, such as the Irish "sídhe" and Welsh "tylwyth teg", and English "fairy" gradually absorbed and blended with these native traditions.

definition: A human-made pile or mound of stones, often built as a landmark, boundary marker, or memorial over a burial site.
origin: Cairn comes from Scottish Gaelic "càrn", a word shared across the Celtic languages for a heap of stones, tracing back to a common Celtic root. Ancient cairns across Ireland, Scotland, and Wales frequently mark Neolithic and Bronze Age burial sites, some, like Newgrange in Ireland, built with such precision that they align with the sunrise on the winter solstice. The tradition of adding a stone to a cairn while passing, "to add to the cairn", survives today as a hiking custom on mountain summits.

definition: In Irish mythology, the fairy folk believed to live within ancient burial mounds, also called the Aos Sí.
origin: Sidhe comes from Irish "sídh" (also spelled "sí"), originally meaning a fairy mound or hill, before extending to name the beings believed to dwell inside it, the "Aos Sí" or "people of the mounds". These mounds were often real Neolithic burial sites, and folk belief held that the Tuatha Dé Danann retreated underground into them after being defeated by later invaders, becoming the sidhe of legend. Disturbing a fairy mound was considered deeply unlucky, a belief so persistent that even modern Irish road projects have occasionally been rerouted around them.

definition: A ghostly, flickering light seen at night over marshes or bogs, said to lure travellers off the safe path.
origin: Will-o'-the-wisp combines the personal name "Will" with "wisp", a bundle of twigs or straw once used as a makeshift torch, painting the light as a mischievous figure carrying his own lantern. The phenomenon has a real scientific explanation, the gentle combustion of gases such as methane released by decaying organic matter in marshland, which produces a pale glow known scientifically as ignis fatuus, Latin for "foolish fire". Folklore across Britain and Ireland cast the light as a trickster spirit or wandering soul, leading unwary night travellers into bogs and danger.

definition: An Irish god of eloquence, poetry, and strength, traditionally credited with inventing the Ogham writing system.
origin: Ogma appears in Old Irish as a member of the Tuatha Dé Danann, sometimes called "Ogma Grianainech" ("sun-faced"), celebrated as a champion warrior as much as a master of language. Some scholars connect his name to the Gaulish god Ogmios, described by the Greek writer Lucian as an old man who drew crowds along by golden chains linked to his tongue, an image of persuasive, binding eloquence.

definition: Short for Tuatha Dé Danann, the mythical race of gods and heroes in Irish mythology said to have ruled Ireland before retreating into the fairy mounds.
origin: Tuatha is the Irish word for "tribe" or "people", combined in "Tuatha Dé Danann" with "dé" (of the god/gods) and "Danann", referring to the goddess Danu, giving the full meaning "the people of the goddess Danu". They were said to have arrived in Ireland in mist-shrouded ships, bringing with them four great treasures including the Spear of Lugh and the Stone of Destiny, and defeated the Fomorians for control of the land. When later human invaders, the Milesians, arrived, the Tuatha Dé Danann agreed to retreat underground into the sídhe, becoming the fairy folk of later legend.

definition: Alluring physical attractiveness or exciting charm; originally, a magic spell cast to alter appearance or perception.
origin: Glamour began as a Scots alteration of "grammar", reflecting a widespread medieval folk belief that learning, especially Latin grammar and the study of arcane books, was closely tied to magic and occult knowledge. By the 18th century, Scots "glamer" or "glamour" specifically meant a spell cast over someone's eyes to make things appear different from what they really were, popularised in the poetry of Sir Walter Scott. Only in the early 20th century did the word soften from an actual bewitching spell into its modern sense of captivating, fashionable charm.

definition: A Welsh word for poetic or artistic inspiration, especially the flowing, divine-seeming gift said to move through bards.
origin: Awen is Old Welsh for "inspiration" or "flowing spirit", likely from a root meaning "to blow" or "breathe", picturing inspiration as a breath or wind moving through the poet. The word appears in the earliest Welsh poetry, including work attributed to the legendary bard Taliesin, who claimed his awen came directly from drinking from a cauldron of wisdom. Modern Welsh cultural life still uses awen as the guiding symbol of the National Eisteddfod, represented by three rays of light at the ceremony's heart.

definition: A legendary sixth-century Welsh bard, part historical poet and part mythical figure, celebrated as the greatest of the early Welsh poets.
origin: Taliesin comes from Welsh "tal" (brow, front) and "iesin" (radiant, shining), together meaning "shining brow", a name legend says was given to him at birth for the light upon his forehead. A real poet of that name likely composed verse in the courts of sixth-century Welsh kings, but medieval tales transformed him into a shapeshifting, prophetic figure who gained all knowledge from three drops of a magic potion brewed by the witch Ceridwen. His legendary life story, the "Hanes Taliesin", blends real early poetry with myth so thoroughly that historians still debate where the man ends and the legend begins.

definition: The queen of Arthurian legend, wife of King Arthur, whose love affair with Sir Lancelot became central to the fall of Camelot in later versions of the story.
origin: Guinevere comes from Welsh "Gwenhwyfar", combining "gwen" (white, fair, blessed) and "hwyfar" (smooth, soft, or possibly phantom, spirit), giving a name often translated as "white phantom" or "white enchantress". She appears in the earliest Welsh Arthurian material as Arthur's queen, but it was the French medieval poet Chrétien de Troyes who developed her romance with Lancelot, reshaping her from a queen of a warband into the tragic centrepiece of courtly love and betrayal familiar today. Later Welsh tradition, intriguingly, hints at three women all named Gwenhwyfar, suggesting the figure absorbed several older tales.

definition: The legendary island of Arthurian legend, sometimes called the Isle of Apples, where King Arthur was taken after his final battle to heal or die.
origin: Avalon first appears in Latin as "Insula Avallonis" in Geoffrey of Monmouth's 12th-century "Historia Regum Britanniae". Most scholars trace the name to Welsh "afal", meaning apple, making Avalon the "Isle of Apples" — a fitting home for a mystical otherworld, since apples carried associations with immortality and the Celtic otherworld long before Arthur's story took shape. Later medieval writers, including Chrétien de Troyes and the authors of the Vulgate Cycle, linked the island with the enchantress Morgan le Fay, who was said to rule it and tend to Arthur's wound.

definition: The legendary sword of King Arthur, symbol of his right to rule, sometimes said to have been given to him by the Lady of the Lake.
origin: Excalibur traces back through French Arthurian romance to Geoffrey of Monmouth's Latin "Caliburnus", which itself derives from the Welsh "Caledfwlch" — likely related to the Irish "Caladbolg", meaning "hard cleft" or "hard lightning". The familiar French spelling was later reshaped by writers who folk-connected it to Latin "chalybs" (steel) and the phrase "ex calce liberatus" (freed from the stone), tying the sword's name to the sword-in-the-stone legend even though that connection is almost certainly a later invention rather than the word's true origin.

definition: The legendary king of Britain, central figure of Arthurian romance, said to have led the defense of Britain and ruled from Camelot with the knights of the Round Table.
origin: The name Arthur is most likely derived from the Roman family name "Artorius", of obscure and possibly pre-Roman origin, worn by a real Romano-British military commander whose exploits may have seeded the later legend. A popular but linguistically weaker theory instead traces it to Welsh "arth" (bear) plus "gwr" (man), giving "bear-man"; most modern scholars favor the Roman origin, though the debate remains genuinely unsettled. Whether or not a single historical figure lies behind him, the literary Arthur was built up over centuries by Welsh, Latin, and French writers into the king of Camelot known today.

definition: A prehistoric megalithic tomb structure made of two or more upright stones supporting a flat capstone.
origin: Dolmen entered English via French antiquarian writing in the 18th and 19th centuries, who took it from Breton "taol maen", literally "stone table" ("taol", table, plus "maen", stone). An older theory linked it instead to Cornish "tolmen" ("hole of stone"), and the two possible origins were sometimes confused by early scholars, but "stone table" is now the more widely accepted source. The structures themselves are far older than the word, built across Neolithic Europe as chamber tombs, many still standing after five thousand years.

definition: A traditional Irish ring featuring two hands clasping a crowned heart, symbolizing love, loyalty, and friendship.
origin: The Claddagh ring takes its name from the Claddagh, a small fishing village just outside Galway city in Ireland, from Irish "An Cladach", meaning "the shore" or "stony beach". The design — two hands holding a crowned heart — is traditionally dated to the 17th century and credited to a local goldsmith, Richard Joyce, though much of that story is folklore layered onto a genuine local craft tradition. The ring became a lasting symbol of Irish identity, worn to signal whether the wearer's heart is taken, engaged, or married depending on which way it faces.

definition: An ancient Irish harvest festival celebrated around the first of August, traditionally associated with games, gatherings, and the god Lugh.
origin: Lughnasadh comes from Old Irish "Lugnasad", combining the god "Lugh" with "násad" (an assembly, especially one held in commemoration, often including games or contests). Medieval Irish tradition held that Lugh founded the festival to honor his foster mother Tailtiu, who died clearing the land for agriculture, tying the celebration to the grain harvest. It survives today, sometimes anglicized as "Lammas" in parts of Britain, and continues to be marked by Celtic-tradition communities as one of the four great quarter-day festivals alongside Samhain, Imbolc, and Beltane.
